runs.text: Made by Arshad · 28-fund review
Where each of the 28 funds stands

Nine funds are heavily exposed to an AI-led sell-off, but AI is not the only threat. Oil lurching on every Iran headline (Brent about $96 on 27 Nov, down from about $118 at the end of October), a yen at almost 160 per dollar, the level that has triggered intervention, a 10-year US yield near 5% (about 4.9% on 27 Nov) with a December Fed hike close to certain, and rising tension around Taiwan each hit different funds. Combining all of these, 11 funds rate High or Very high overall risk. Only the money market funds and cash are close to safe in every scenario.
Why these 28:

together they form a comprehensive set covering cash in three currencies, government and corporate bonds, developed and emerging-market shares, real estate, commodities, gold and absolute return, across the US, Europe, the UK, Japan, Asia and the Pacific. Almost any market event shows up somewhere in the list.

Insight USD Liquidity (14) and the USD cash account (10) for USD-based investors; Insight EUR (15) for EUR-based investors. Insight USD yields about 4% with daily liquidity.

US Treasuries (28) and the global bond funds (9, 25, 26) should rise if a crash pushes the Fed to cut. They fell this year because war-driven inflation pushed yields up, so they guard against a growth shock, not an inflation shock.

The yen funds (11, 27) are a currency bet with the yen near ¥158. The commodity fund (12) would fall if an Iran deal reopens Hormuz. Europe (5) is exposed to French debt stress, and the Asian funds (22, 23, 24) to Taiwan tension and currency outflows.
UK (8), Pacific (7) and Fulcrum (16), then Europe ex-UK (5) and Japan (27). Gold miners (1) and commodities (12) are not AI-driven but can still fall 25–40% in a general liquidation.
Update · Sat 28 Nov 2026, 6 am Manila (covers Fri 27 Nov)
Wall Street capped its best week in over a year as Chinese chip stocks posted a record jump

Wall Street ended a shortened Friday session strongly. The S&P 500 rose 1.6% to 7,298, capping its best week in over a year (+5.6%), though it is still on course for its worst November since 2008. Asia surged first: Chinese chip stocks had their biggest one-day gain on record after Beijing pledged market support, and Korea's KOSPI jumped 4.3%. Gold rebounded from a 15-month low. Brent held near $96 before Sunday's OPEC+ meeting, and the 10-year yield rose to about 4.9%. S&P's France rating decision had not been reported when this was written. The S&P 500 is now about 6.7% below its record. No fund rating changed.

cells.text: What happened
Funds affected
What it means
Best US week in over a year.

In a session that ended at 1 pm New York time on Friday, the S&P 500 rose 1.61% to 7,298.34, the Nasdaq 2.31% to 24,129.50 and the Dow 1.19% to 50,780.64 (Reuters via World Today Journal). For the week the S&P 500 gained about 5.6%, the Nasdaq about 6.7% and the chip index about 9.3%. NVIDIA rose 0.8% on Friday to $150.49, up about 20% on the week but still 37% below its October record, and Micron jumped 7.6% (The Glass Desk). The S&P 500 and Nasdaq were still on course for their worst November since 2008 (Reuters via World Today Journal).

The North America, Shariah, climate and Developed World funds (6, 13, 19, 4, 3) won back a large part of November's losses. Jensen Huang's House and Senate appearances next week could test this rebound.
Chinese chip stocks had a record day; Korea and Japan jumped.

China's State Council promised stronger market support, including a bigger role for state investors and more insurance and pension money in shares. A 40-stock chip index rose 17.6%, its largest one-day gain on record, and the Shanghai Composite rose 3.73% to 3,606.49 (Asia Daily). Korea's KOSPI rose 4.34% to 4,915.68, Japan's Nikkei 2.11% to 58,711, Taiwan 0.4% and Hong Kong about 2.1–2.2% (NERO, citing Reuters, Yonhap and Yahoo Finance; sources differ on Hong Kong). Europe's STOXX 600 rose 1% to 643.85, with miners up 3.5% or more; it gained nearly 3% on the week but is still down for November (QNC News).

The emerging-market and Asian funds (22, 24) gain most, since they hold Chinese, Korean and Taiwanese chipmakers. Japan (27), Pacific (7), Europe (5) and the UK (8) also rose. Policy-driven rallies in China have often faded within weeks.
Gold rebounded; yields and the dollar edged up.

Spot gold rose 2.3% to about $3,648 an ounce and gold futures about 3.9% to $3,674.50, after a 15-month low earlier in the week (The Private Banker, The Glass Desk). The 10-year Treasury yield rose to about 4.89–4.92% (sources differ), from about 4.85% on Wednesday, and futures put a December Fed hike at about 98–99%. The dollar was about 159.4–159.5 yen and the euro about $1.095 (NERO, The Private Banker). Tokyo core inflation rose to 2.9% in November, just below forecasts, keeping a Bank of Japan hike at its 17–18 Dec meeting in play (NERO, Wisevoter).

Gold miners (1) got a lift, but one strong day does not end gold's correction. Slightly higher yields hold back the bond funds (28, 9, 25, 26), while the money market funds (14, 11) keep earning more. The yen funds (11, 27) stay just below 160, the level where Japan has stepped in before.
Oil held near $96 before OPEC+.

January Brent traded around $96.30 on Friday afternoon (London time), after Thursday's $96.57 settle, its highest since 6 Nov, and was up about 4% on the week; the February contract was about $91.90 (FinanceFeeds). A projectile hit Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery on Thursday, briefly halting part of it (Reuters via BigGo Finance). Sources told Reuters that OPEC+ has agreed in principle to keep output targets unchanged in early 2027 (FinanceFeeds), while Iraq is pressing for a higher capacity estimate (Wisevoter).

Oil near $96 supports the commodity fund (12) and the UK fund's energy companies (8), but keeps inflation pressure on bonds (28). A rollover on Sunday would likely change little; a surprise could move oil sharply.
Coming up (Manila):

S&P Global's France review was due after Europe's close on Friday; no result had appeared in the reports found for this update, and AFP had called an outlook cut the most likely outcome (Boursorama). Sun 29 Nov: OPEC+ meets on 2027 output. Tue 1 Dec (US time): Jensen Huang has closed-door House interviews; Thu 3 Dec (US time): he testifies to the Senate Banking Committee. Fri 4 Dec, 9:30 pm: US November jobs report. Thu 10 Dec, about 3 am: Fed decision. Thu 17 Dec, evening: ECB and Bank of England decisions; 17–18 Dec: Bank of Japan meeting.

France's rating matters for the euro funds (5, 15, 18, 21) and OPEC+ for the commodity fund (12). Huang's testimony and the jobs report steer the AI funds (6, 13) and the bond funds (28, 9) before the Fed. The Bank of Japan meeting matters for the yen funds (11, 27).

Earlier updates
With Wall Street shut for Thanksgiving, Asia and Europe bounced back; Korea raised rates and oil climbed again.
On 26 Nov the STOXX 600 rose 1.8% and Taiwan 2.5%, the Bank of Korea raised its rate to 3.25%, and Brent rose to roughly $95–96 as more tankers were hit near Hormuz. No change.
A hot inflation reading and new tariff plans sank AI stocks, but Wall Street clawed back most of the drop.

On 25 Nov October core inflation (PCE) was 3.3% and growth was revised up to 4.3%; chip stocks fell more than 6% and Korea and Taiwan about 6%, but the S&P 500 closed only 0.25% lower, about 8.1% below its record. No change.
The NVIDIA relief rally faded as AI stocks slid again, while the Dow rose.

On 24 Nov NVIDIA fell about 6%, the chip index about 9% and Anthropic below its $83 IPO price; the S&P 500 closed 0.5% lower at 7,201.09 and the Nasdaq 1.5% lower, while the Dow gained 0.85% (closing figures, revised from late-session estimates). No change.
Jensen Huang returned to NVIDIA and Wall Street had its best day since April 2025.

On 23 Nov NVIDIA rose about 31.5% and the S&P 500 about 4.7% to roughly 7,237 (closing figures, revised from earlier estimates of 33% and 5.0%), while Brent fell to a two-week low and the euro hit a 2026 low. No change.
Iran hit two more supertankers as Hormuz attacks neared a record month.

On 22 Nov Iran said two supertankers hit mines east of the strait, at least 22 attacks on shipping had been reported in November, and Wall Street had ended the previous week with the VIX at 35.89. No change.
Iran stepped up attacks on Hormuz tankers and Bahrain before a short Thanksgiving week.

On 21 Nov two tankers leaving the strait were hit by projectiles off Oman, Iran said another hit a mine, and Bahrain intercepted Iranian air attacks; Qatari mediation produced no deal, and Brent had ended the week at $92.57. No change.
S&P 500 and Dow closed in a correction as the AI rout deepened; the Nasdaq turned negative for 2026.
On 20 Nov the S&P 500 fell 3.7% to 6,910.39, about 11.6% below its record, with NVIDIA down 14% and gold about 4.5%; the 10-year yield fell to about 4.91% as investors sought safety. No change.
Anthropic jumped 17% on its debut, but the S&P 500 fell 2% for a sixth day, 8.2% below its record.
Gold fell about 2% to a 14-month low and Taiwan about 4.4%, while Fed Governor Waller pushed for aggressive action in December. No change.
NVIDIA beat forecasts but its shares fell; the S&P 500 dropped for a fifth day, 6.4% below its record.
On 18 Nov Fed minutes pointed to a December hike, US crude fell 3–4% on a surprise rise in stockpiles, and gold fell about 3%. No change.
Stocks slid again before NVIDIA's results; the S&P 500 fell 1.2%, 6.3% below its record, and Korea closed below 5,000.
On 17 Nov the Dow fell 1.6%, software stocks led the losses, US retail sales beat forecasts and a December Fed hike was about 95% priced. No change.
New US chip curbs sank AI stocks a day before NVIDIA's results; the S&P 500 fell 1.9%, back more than 5% below its record.
The chip index fell about 4.6% and Taiwan about 6%, while Brent fell 3.6% to $92.44 on the IEA's surplus forecast. No change.
Iran said a supertanker sank in Hormuz and its drones targeted Bahrain; NVIDIA results and Anthropic's debut lined up a decisive week.
Over the weekend Saudi Arabia intercepted Houthi missiles and drones and the G7 condemned Iran's attacks; Brent had closed Friday near $96. No change.
Wall Street posted its first up week in five, but NVIDIA fell for a sixth week; Iran said three tankers hit mines.
On 13 Nov the S&P 500 fell 0.4% to 7,561.67 but gained about 2.5% on the week, the 10-year yield closed near 5.15%, and Brent settled near $95.84. No change.
Chip stocks slid again as NVIDIA's leadership crisis dragged on; US producer prices rose 6.5% on a year.
In Friday afternoon trading on 13 Nov the chip index was down about 3.7%, AMD about 10.6% and the S&P 500 about 0.5–0.8%, and the 10-year yield touched 5.17%. No change.
NVIDIA's CEO Jensen Huang resigned; oil jumped as Trump said no Iran deal is needed.
On 12 Nov NVIDIA fell as much as 14% and closed about 4.3% lower, the S&P 500 slipped 0.4% to about 7,592, and the 10-year yield rose to about 5.1%. No change.
Chip stocks bounced back as CoreWeave calmed AI-spending fears.
On 11 Nov the chip index rose about 7% and the S&P 500 about 1.3% to roughly 7,620, with NVIDIA up about 3.5%. Brent rose about 1% to $92.5 as Iran denied talks. No change.
Hotter US inflation pushed the 10-year yield back above 5%, and NVIDIA sank.

On 10 Nov October consumer prices rose 0.4% in the month, making a December Fed hike close to fully priced. The S&P 500 slipped 0.4% to about 7,520 and NVIDIA fell 5.5–6.3% (sources differ), after Asia had rallied. No change.
Wall Street jumped 2.3% as chips rebounded and oil sank, but NVIDIA fell on a probe of its CEO.
On 9 Nov the S&P 500 rose to 7,550 and the chip index about 7%, while NVIDIA fell 4.4% and Brent dropped to about $93–94. No change.
Asia opened split, then Korea turned higher.
The Nikkei opened 2% higher while the KOSPI briefly fell below 5,000 on foreign selling, then recovered to 5,113 as SK Hynix and Samsung rebounded. Brent eased to about $97. No change.

AI-crash scenario
Who gets hurt, who holds

In an AI-led crash I estimate the most AI-concentrated funds could fall 30–40%, broad developed-market equity funds 20–30%, and cash would hold its value. Government bonds would likely gain a few percent, but only if the crash lowers inflation fears rather than arriving with another oil shock.

My estimates from each fund's AI concentration, equity beta and volatility, calibrated to the 2000–02 dot-com bust (S&P 500 about −49%), 2022 (MSCI World −18%, US Treasuries −13%) and Korea's July 2026 chip crash (KOSPI −40% in six weeks). Not forecasts.
Scenario assumed.

AI capital spending is cut sharply, US mega-cap tech falls 40–50%, the S&P 500 falls 25–35% and Asian chip stocks repeat their July 2026 slide. The Fed responds by cutting rates. If inflation stays high instead (for example, the Strait of Hormuz closes again), the bond funds would not rise and only cash would hold.
Liquidity.
Every fund deals daily; settlement is typically 1–3 business days plus any platform processing time. In a crash the practical risks are:
Emerging-market and Asian equity funds (22, 24) and the commodity swap fund (12) can see prices gap and dealing spreads widen.
Funds can apply swing pricing or, in extreme cases, defer large redemptions; this matters most for the active and EM funds.
Selling after a fall locks in the loss. The 2000–02 and 2022 sell-offs both had sharp rebounds that punished late sellers.

Real estate (2), Japan (27), commodities (12): moderate to high volatility with partial AI or rate exposure.
Developed World (3, 4), NT Climate (19), North America (6): broad but AI-heavy.
Robeco EM (22), HSBC Islamic (13), Schroder Asian Opportunities (24), World Gold miners (1): the most volatile; the first three are the most AI-exposed of the 28 funds.
Beyond AI
Eight other risks in the news now, and which funds they hit
An AI crash is one way to lose money; these are the others. Several are already moving markets this month. Numbers link to each fund's analysis.
Green
marks a fund that would likely benefit.
1 · Yen turmoil

The yen fell to about 163 per dollar in late July, prompting a joint US–Japan intervention (Japan reportedly spent around $85bn) that pushed it to 155. By mid-August most of that gain had reversed. It was near 158 on 27 Oct, and Finance Minister Katayama has warned she is ready to act again, with traders watching 160. The pressures are a slow Bank of Japan (held at 1.25% on 30 Oct, though it signalled more hikes), PM Takaichi's 19 Oct signal that about ¥10 trillion of tax cuts may be funded with deficit bonds (debt is 204% of GDP), 10-year JGB yields near 3%, and an oil import bill that has only just started to ease (Brent near $98 on 6 Nov, from $115 in late October). On 12–13 Nov the dollar reached about 159.8–159.9 yen, the closest yet to 160. On 16 Nov it was near 159.6 after Japan reported that its economy shrank at a 0.1% annual rate in July–September. On 19 Nov it was about 159.5 as the dollar index hit a 19-month high, on 23 Nov it was near 159.3, and on 25 Nov about 159.3 again. The move can run either way: intervention or a carry-trade unwind could lift the yen 5% in days. On 26 Nov it was about 159.25 in quiet holiday trade. On 27 Nov the yen was about 159.4–159.5 per dollar, and Tokyo core inflation rose to 2.9%.

2 · Oil shock and the Strait of Hormuz

Brent settled at $115.32 on 28 Oct. At least 22 attacks were reported in November by 22 Nov, after more than 30 in October. On 23 Nov Brent fell about 2.2% to $90.55, a two-week low, as Middle East supplies rose and Libya's Sharara pipeline restarted, despite a Houthi claim of an attack on a Saudi refinery and an Iranian strike on Bahrain over the weekend. On 24 Nov Brent hovered near $89, close to three-month lows, and the US was reported to be probing cyberattacks on up to 50 tankers. On 25 Nov Brent rose about 3–3.5% to roughly $93–94 after Saudi forces intercepted four drones aimed at the Ras Tanura refinery and Iran reported more tankers hitting mines; OPEC+ meets on 29 Nov. Traffic is about 65% below pre-war levels, and Qatari mediation has produced no deal. Nothing is agreed, and the strait has been largely closed since March. This is a two-way risk. A deal could send oil sharply lower; Brent fell to about $72 during the brief June truce. A longer closure keeps inflation and rates high. On 26 Nov Brent rose to roughly $95–96 as Iran said two more tankers hit mines near Khasab; ANZ put Hormuz flows at about half of normal. On 27 Nov Brent held near $96 after a projectile hit Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery; OPEC+ is expected to keep its targets unchanged on 29 Nov.

3 · Sticky inflation and rising bond yields

US CPI rose to 3.7% in September (core 2.6%). The Fed held on 28 Oct in a 10–2 vote, with both dissenters wanting a hike. The 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.35%, the highest since 2002. On 10 Nov October CPI rose 0.4% in the month (core 0.3%), above forecasts; the 10-year yield jumped to about 5.01%, a December hike became close to fully priced, and Fed Governor Waller said a half-point move could be considered. On 18 Nov minutes of the October meeting showed nearly all officials expect a December hike. Over the week to 20 Nov the 10-year yield fell to 4.92% from 5.15% and the 2-year to 4.63% from 4.88%. On 23 Nov, as stocks rebounded, CME FedWatch showed about 98% odds of a quarter-point December hike and bets on a half point had faded; the 10-year yield was about 4.94%. On 25 Nov October core inflation (PCE) was 3.3%, above the 3.2% forecast, and third-quarter growth was revised up to 4.3%; even so the 10-year yield fell about 8 bp to 4.85% as stocks slid, and December hike odds stayed at about 92–98%. Rising yields hurt bonds, REITs and expensive growth stocks at the same time, as in 2022. On 26 Nov the Bank of Korea raised its rate to 3.25%, and ECB minutes showed many members were open to a hike. On 27 Nov the 10-year yield rose to about 4.9%, with a December Fed hike priced at about 98–99%.

4 · French debt stress and a weaker euro

France's 10-year yield hit 4.98% on 21 Oct, a 24-year high, and its spread over Germany reached 157 bp, the widest since the euro crisis. EUR/USD fell 3.9% between 9 Sep and 23 Oct even though the ECB raised rates twice this year to 2.50%. Eurozone inflation is 3.8%, and the October PMI fell to a four-month low. On 29 Oct the ECB held, the euro touched a 17-month low, and Lagarde's early exit (7 Feb 2027, before the French election) was confirmed. On 18 Nov the euro fell to about $1.096, its lowest since April 2025. On 19 Nov it stayed near $1.096, and Germany's DAX fell about 1.1%. On 23 Nov France's flash composite PMI fell to 46.2, against 47.8 expected, and the euro dropped to about $1.0884, a new 2026 low; markets put about 91% odds on an ECB hike to 2.75% on 17 Dec, and S&P Global reviews France's A+ rating on 27 Nov. On 25 Nov the France–Germany 10-year spread was about 1.51 points; S&P's decision was due after Europe's close on 27 Nov; no result had been reported by early 28 Nov, Manila time.

5 · Taiwan tension and Asian currency stress

China held live-fire drills across five sea areas on 12–17 Oct, coast-guard ships harassed Taiwanese vessels on 18 Oct, and on 16 Oct Beijing drafted export curbs on about 40 technologies, including AI and chips. On 15 Oct foreign investors sold NT$165bn of Taiwan stocks in one day, Korean outflows for October passed $10bn, the Philippine peso passed 63 per dollar for the first time, and India and Indonesia intervened to support their currencies. On 16 Nov the US tightened rules on Chinese access to advanced AI chips, including through overseas data centres, and Taiwan's market fell about 6%. On 17 Nov Taiwan fell another 2.3% and Korea's KOSPI 2.6% to a six-month low. On 18 Nov the KOSPI rebounded about 1.9% to back above 5,000, and Taiwan edged up 0.1%, after NVIDIA's results. On 19 Nov Taiwan fell about 4.4% and the MSCI Asia-Pacific ex-Japan index hit a seven-month low, while Korea rose 1.4%. On 20 Nov Taiwan fell about 5.7% and Korea about 5.2%, putting Taiwan on course for its steepest weekly fall since October 1997. On 25 Nov Taiwan fell more than 6% and TSMC about 8% as the AI sell-off returned. On 27 Nov Taiwan rose only 0.4% while Chinese chip stocks had a record one-day jump on Beijing's pledge of market support.

6 · AI debt inside "safe" bond funds

AI-related borrowing has passed roughly $466–500bn this year and makes up about 10% of the largest long-term investment-grade bond ETFs. Oracle's 5-year CDS more than doubled to about 308 bp, Meta's and NVIDIA's hit records in October, and CoreWeave's implies a default probability above 60%. On 28 Oct Alphabet reported that its long-term debt had jumped from $46.5bn to $125.1bn in a year, alongside $12.4bn of stock sales, to pay for AI. On 5 Nov the chip index fell 12.3% and the Nasdaq entered correction, as investors priced a slower, costlier AI build-out. On 19 Nov Anthropic raised a record $81.3bn in its IPO and its shares closed 17% above the $83 offer price, but CoreWeave swung from a 10.5% gain to a loss of about 5.5% as AI stocks slid again. On 20 Nov the AI sell-off deepened: NVIDIA fell 14%, AMD 13% and Anthropic 8.5%. On 23 Nov NVIDIA reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO and AI stocks surged: NVIDIA rose about 31.5% and CoreWeave about 24% during the day. On 24 Nov the rally faded: NVIDIA fell about 7–8%, CoreWeave about 12% and Anthropic about 13% to roughly $76, below its IPO price. On 25 Nov S&P put NVIDIA's AA credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade, citing governance.

7 · UK Budget and gilts

The 10-year gilt yield touched 5.53% on 8 Oct, the highest since 2007. UK inflation is 3.5%, and markets expect a Bank of England hike on 5 Nov. The 28 Oct Budget kept about £15bn of fiscal headroom and gilts held steady, but it doubled the bank surcharge to 6%, a cost for the UK fund's banks. On 18 Nov UK inflation figures showed prices rising faster, and the 10-year gilt yield fell about 0.08 points to 5.29% as oil dropped. On 26 Nov the 10-year gilt yield was about 5.15%.

8 · Gold's correction and Australia's rate hikes

Gold briefly fell below $4,000 on 23 Oct, about a quarter under its January record. It dropped alongside stocks as leveraged investors raised cash, so it did not behave as a safe haven that day. It slipped again on 29 Oct and fell 3.3% to a one-year low of $3,899 on 30 Oct as tech sold off, just above Standard Chartered's $3,886 warning level. On 12 Nov it fell about 2.9% to roughly $3,885 as the dollar firmed on Fed hike bets. On 20 Nov it fell about 4.5% to roughly $3,519 (futures), its lowest since September 2025. On 23 Nov it bounced about 4.2% to roughly $3,663 as stocks rallied. On 25 Nov it touched about $3,426, its lowest since September 2025, before recovering. In Australia, the RBA has hiked four times this year to 4.60%, CPI is 4.0%, and Q3 core inflation of 3.7% beat forecasts on 28 Oct, and on 3 Nov the RBA hiked a fifth time to 4.85%, the highest since 2008, in a split 6–3 vote that dropped its tightening bias. On 19 Nov the Australian dollar hit a 10-month low after weak jobs data. On 25 Nov October inflation rose to 4.9%, above forecasts, adding pressure for another hike. On 27 Nov gold rebounded about 2–4% to roughly $3,650–3,675 an ounce from a 15-month low.

November so far. The 3 Nov midterms, in which Democrats won both houses of Congress, set off the sharpest AI sell-off of the year on worries about slower data-centre building. On 5 Nov the chip index fell 12%, its worst day since 2020, and the Nasdaq entered a correction. In the week to 6 Nov the S&P 500 lost 2.7% and the Nasdaq 3.4% (AP); Japan's Nikkei lost 9.3%, leaving it more than 20% below its June record (Yahoo Finance), and Korea's KOSPI 11.7% (Seoul Economic Daily). Brent fell about 16% on hopes of a US–Iran deal (CNBC), while a strong jobs report kept a December Fed hike likely (InvestmentNews). On 9 Nov Wall Street rebounded: the S&P 500 rose 2.3% and the chip index about 7%, while NVIDIA fell 4.4% on a board probe of its CEO and Brent dropped to about $93–94 (Reuters). On 10 Nov hotter October inflation (0.4% in the month) pushed the 10-year yield to about 5.01% and the S&P 500 down about 0.4%, with NVIDIA down 6.3%; Asia had rallied, with the KOSPI up 4% (AP). On 11 Nov chip stocks rebounded about 7% after CoreWeave's results, lifting the S&P 500 about 1.3% to roughly 7,620 (Reuters). On 12 Nov NVIDIA's CEO Jensen Huang resigned; NVIDIA fell as much as 14% before paring losses, the S&P 500 slipped 0.4% to about 7,592, and Brent rose after Trump said no Iran deal is needed (Kiplinger, AP). On 13 Nov chip stocks slid again (chip index about −3.4%, NVIDIA −2.0%) and the S&P 500 closed 0.4% lower at 7,561.67, but it still gained about 2.5% for the week, its first weekly gain in five; October producer prices were up 6.5% on a year, and the 10-year yield closed near 5.15% (Yahoo Finance, CappNotes). Over the weekend Iran said a supertanker sank after hitting a mine in the strait, and drone and missile attacks on Bahrain and Saudi Arabia were intercepted (AFP via RTÉ, Gulf News). On 16 Nov new US curbs on Chinese access to advanced chips sent the chip index down about 4.6% and the S&P 500 about 1.9% to roughly 7,415, more than 5% below its record, while Brent fell 3.6% to $92.44 on the IEA's surplus forecast (Reuters, Bloomberg). On 17 Nov stocks fell again before NVIDIA's results: the S&P 500 lost 1.2% to about 7,327, about 6.3% below its record, and Korea's KOSPI closed below 5,000 for the first time since February (Reuters, AP). On 18 Nov NVIDIA's revenue beat forecasts at $115.8bn, but its shares fell about 3%; the S&P 500 slipped about 0.3% for a fifth straight fall while the Dow lost about 1.2%, and US crude fell 3–4% and gold about 3% (Wealth Professional, Yahoo Finance, Bloomberg). On 19 Nov Anthropic's record $81.3bn IPO opened 34% above its $83 price and closed up 17%, but an early rally faded and the S&P 500 fell 2.0% to 7,175.83, a sixth straight loss and 8.2% below its record, while gold fell to a 14-month low (Yahoo Finance, AP). On 20 Nov the S&P 500 fell 3.7% to 6,910.39, a seventh straight loss, and closed in a correction about 11.6% below its record; the Nasdaq lost 5.3% and turned negative for 2026, NVIDIA fell 14%, and gold fell about 4.5% (Yahoo Finance, CBS News). In the week to 20 Nov the S&P 500 fell 8.6%, the Nasdaq 10.0% and the Dow 8.0%, while the 10-year yield fell to 4.92% (The Closing Print). On 21 Nov Iran stepped up attacks on tankers near Hormuz and on Bahrain (AP, Gulf News). On 22 Nov Iran said two supertankers hit mines east of the strait, and at least 22 attacks on shipping had been reported in November (Middle East Eye, SSBCrack). On 23 Nov NVIDIA reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO; NVIDIA rose about 31.5%, the S&P 500 about 4.7% and the Nasdaq about 6.5%, the best day for US stocks since April 2025, while Brent fell to a two-week low near $90.5 and the euro hit a 2026 low (TipRanks, Reuters, TradingNews). On 24 Nov the AI rally faded: NVIDIA fell about 7–8%, the chip index about 9% and Anthropic below its IPO price, while the Dow rose about 0.6% on strong consumer confidence; late in the session the S&P 500 was about 7,175, about 8.2% below its record, and the 10-year yield 4.90% (Reuters, Yahoo Finance, Bloomberg). On 25 Nov October core inflation of 3.3% and new US tariff proposals hit AI stocks again: the S&P 500 fell as much as 2.9% and the Nasdaq 100 briefly entered a bear market, but by the close the S&P 500 was down only 0.25%, about 8.1% below its record, and the 10-year yield had fallen to 4.85% (TipRanks, Fox Business, Longbridge). On 26 Nov, with US markets shut for Thanksgiving, Asia and Europe rebounded (STOXX 600 +1.8%) and the Bank of Korea raised rates to 3.25% (AP, JBizNews). On 27 Nov the S&P 500 rose 1.6% to 7,298.34 in a shortened session, ending its best week in over a year (+5.6%) about 6.7% below its record, as Chinese chip stocks had a record one-day gain (The Glass Desk, Asia Daily).

In an inflationary environment stocks and bonds can fall together, as in 2022. If an AI crash instead triggers a growth scare and Fed cuts, Treasuries and high-quality bonds should rally. Which of those two worlds arrives decides whether the bond funds protect you; only the cash-like funds are safe in both.

Buying in a sell-off
If the S&P 500 falls 5%, 10% or 20%: which funds to add

A guide to which of the 28 funds tend to be worth adding as a sell-off deepens, using the S&P 500's fall from its 7,819 record (6 Oct 2026) as the trigger, because it is the market's main gauge. The idea is to add the steadier, low-AI funds first and the high-growth, AI-heavy funds only once they are much cheaper. Purchases are funded mainly from cash and from bonds that have risen. Where we are now: on Friday 27 Nov (US time), in a shortened session, the S&P 500 rose 1.6% to 7,298.34, about 6.7% below its record, ending its best week in over a year. It is still below the −5% level (~7,430), first crossed on 5 Nov, and would need to rise about 1.8% to get back above it. It closed below the −10% level (~7,040) on 20 Nov but is now about 3.7% above it. The −20% level (~6,255) is about 14% lower.

In an AI or growth crash, Treasuries usually rise, so selling some bonds to buy stocks works. In an oil or inflation shock, bonds may fall too: fund purchases from cash (14) instead, and consider trimming the commodity fund (12), which is likely to have risen.

AI-crash estimates
are my judgement, not model output or forecasts.
Volatility 1–7
(shown as "Risk 1–7" in the earlier version) is my rating on the familiar SRI scale for how much each fund's price swings; it is not the official KID rating.
Other key risks
are non-AI threats backed by news from 4–26 October 2026: currencies, oil, inflation and rates, sovereign debt, geopolitics and credit. Each is rated Low, Medium or High for that fund.
Overall risk

combines AI exposure, those other risks and volatility into one judgement, on a scale from Very low to Very high, for an investor whose spending currency is the US dollar. Funds 11 and 15 carry a note because their risk is much lower in their own currency. These ratings are my judgement and will change with the news; the dates to watch are listed under Other risks.
